passage: Monday: Dolma's blue blanket, the one she took everywhere, went into the washing machine. She stood at the glass door and cried. Tuesday: Her mother Ritu sat on the floor beside her. "You miss it. It was your soft one." Dolma nodded and leaned against her. Ritu did not say "it's only a blanket." Wednesday: The blanket was dry and smelled of soap, not of Dolma. She held it, frowning. "It's different." "It is," said Ritu. "We can make it yours again." Dolma took it to bed.

qa.q: What colour was Dolma's blanket?
qa.a: Dolma's blanket was blue.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when she stood at the glass door and cried?
qa.a: Dolma was sad and worried about losing her comfort, since the blanket was her soft one she took everywhere.

qa.q: What did Ritu do that helped Dolma grieve without dismissing the loss?
qa.a: Ritu sat on the floor and named the feeling, saying Dolma missed it. Ritu did not say it's only a blanket.

qa.q: How might Ritu have felt watching Dolma cry over the washing machine?
qa.a: Ritu was probably tender and patient, and understood that the blanket mattered to Dolma even though it was just being washed.

grounding: A child cries when a favourite blanket is washed; honouring the loss briefly works better than saying it is only a blanket.

passage:
The platform was crowded and loud, and the train was due in ten minutes. Aadhya's toy giraffe, held tight, slipped from her hand and its neck snapped on the concrete. She stared, then wailed.
Her father Wasim knelt among the bags and legs. He didn't say "It's only a toy." He said, "Your giraffe broke. That's so sad." Aadhya buried her face in his shoulder. When the sobbing eased, he put the pieces carefully in his jacket pocket. "We'll fix it when we get home."
On the train she asked, "Can we use glue?"
"Yes."

qa.q: How long until the train was due?
qa.a: The train was due in ten minutes.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when the giraffe's neck snapped?
qa.a: Aadhya was shocked and heartbroken, staring at first and then wailing.

qa.q: What did Wasim do that respected the loss even on a busy platform?
qa.a: Wasim knelt down, named the sadness, let Aadhya cry on his shoulder and kept the pieces safe in his pocket with a promise to fix it.

qa.q: How might Wasim have felt kneeling among the bags with the train coming?
qa.a: Wasim was probably pressed for time, but chose to stop and comfort Aadhya first, showing care.

grounding: A child cries when a favourite toy breaks; honouring the loss briefly beats saying it is only a toy.

passage:
"My train! Didi, the wheel came off!" Francis held up the little blue engine, crying.
Sarika knelt beside him. "Oh no. Your favourite engine."
"It's broken forever!"
"It looks really broken," she said. "You're so sad."
"It went with me everywhere."
"I know. To Nani's house. On the bus." She hugged him. "It's okay to be sad."
Francis sniffed. "Can we keep it anyway?"
"Of course. Where should it live?"
"In my special box."
They put the engine in his box together. Francis patted the lid. "Bye, engine." Then he went to play.

qa.q: What colour was Francis's engine?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: How can you tell Francis felt sad about the train?
qa.a: He cried, said it was broken forever, and said it went with him everywhere.

qa.q: What did Sarika do that helped Francis let go?
qa.a: She named his sadness, hugged him, and helped him give the engine a special place and say goodbye, instead of calling it just a toy.

qa.q: What would change if Sarika had said 'It's only a toy'?
qa.a: Francis might have felt his sadness didn't matter and found it harder to let go.

grounding: Shows a young child crying over a broken favourite toy and an older sister honouring the loss briefly before he moves on.

passage:
Nursery note, Tuesday.
Sonali (4) arrived in tears. Her yellow blanket, the one she naps with every day, was lost on the train last night. She couldn't settle at circle time. Nilesh told her, "It's only a blanket," and she cried harder.
I sat with her in the reading corner and said losing something special is really sad, and it's okay to miss it. She said it smelled like home. We drew the blanket together and pinned the picture by her nap mat.
By lunch she was playing again. I told her mother at pickup.

qa.q: Where was Sonali's blanket lost?
qa.a: On the train last night.

qa.q: What was Sonali feeling at circle time?
qa.a: She was sad and upset, unable to settle after losing the blanket she naps with every day.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped Sonali let go?
qa.a: They sat with her, said it was okay to miss it, and drew a picture of the blanket together to honour it.

qa.q: How might Nilesh have meant 'It's only a blanket'?
qa.a: Nilesh probably meant to help, without understanding how special the blanket felt to Sonali.

grounding: Shows a young child grieving a lost comfort blanket and an adult honouring the loss briefly, helping her move on.

passage: In the village near Ujjain, Aditi, five, made a clay doll and left it on the courtyard wall to dry. At night the rain came. In the morning, the doll was a brown puddle. Aditi wailed. Her big brother Gautam didn't laugh. He crouched next to her. "Your doll melted. That's really sad." "She had a red bindi!" "I remember." Aditi cried a little more. Gautam helped her scoop the mud into a small pot. "We can plant a flower in her," he said. Aditi nodded, wiping her eyes, and pressed a seed in.

qa.q: What happened to Aditi's clay doll?
qa.a: It melted into a brown puddle in the rain.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel when she saw the doll?
qa.a: She was heartbroken and upset, wailing at the loss.

qa.q: How did Gautam help Aditi let go?
qa.a: He named her sadness, remembered the doll with her, and turned the mud into a flower pot, honouring the loss briefly.

qa.q: What was it like for Gautam to see his sister cry?
qa.a: He seemed caring and gentle, choosing not to laugh and helping her feel better.

grounding: Shows a young child mourning a lost clay doll and an older brother honouring the loss before helping her move on.

passage: In their flat in Malmö, Valentina's rabbit came out of the washing machine with one ear gone. She held the soggy rabbit and howled. Her big brother Oskar said, "It's only a toy," and Pappa gave him a look. Pappa sat down on the floor. "Ruby lost her ear. That's really sad. You've had her since you were a baby." They searched the machine together, but the ear was gone. "Shall we give her a new one, or keep her like this?" Valentina thought. "A new one. A purple one." Ten minutes later she was choosing thread.

qa.q: What happened to the rabbit in the washing machine?
qa.a: It came out with one ear gone.

qa.q: How did Valentina feel when she saw Ruby's missing ear?
qa.a: She felt heartbroken and upset 😢 holding the soggy rabbit and howling.

qa.q: Why did Pappa's response help more than "It's only a toy"?
qa.a: He named the loss and how long she had had Ruby, so Valentina felt understood and could move on to choosing a new ear.

qa.q: Why might Oskar have said "It's only a toy"?
qa.a: He may have meant to calm her, not realising that to his little sister Ruby was far more than a toy.

grounding: Shows a young child grieving a damaged favourite toy and a parent honouring the loss briefly before helping her move on.
